title: Existence and spectral instability of steady rolls in the Nikolaevskiy equation: a computer-assisted study
authors: Nikita V. Konev, Fedor A. Vyazanitsyn, Igor A. Knyazev
abstract: The Nikolaevskiy equation is a model of short-wave pattern formation coupled to a neutral long-wave mode, and it is believed that all of its spatially periodic steady states are unstable. Existing results are formal, numerical, or restricted to a small neighbourhood of onset. We give computer-assisted proofs of three results. First, for every wavenumber q in [0.9, 1.1] and every control parameter r between the onset value (1-q^2)^2 and 4, the equation has a nontrivial, real-analytic, odd steady roll; these rolls form a single continuous two-parameter family that bifurcates from the trivial state at onset, with an explicit amplitude bound proportional to the square root of the distance to onset. Second, every roll of this family with r in [0.25, 4] is spectrally unstable on the real line: its linearisation has a Bloch eigenvalue with real part at least 6.7e-4, and at least 0.13 for r >= 0.575. Third, at nine sample points we enclose, at a small Bloch number, the eigenvalue numerically identified with the long-wave (Matthews-Cox) branch; its real part is positive at seven points and negative at two, while strongly unstable eigenvalues exist at all nine. The proofs combine a parametrised Newton-Kantorovich theorem, a desingularisation near onset, Taylor-model bounds on parameter boxes, and a Weyl-sequence argument for the Bloch spectrum; all estimates are evaluated in rigorous interval arithmetic.
summary: This paper rigorously proves the existence of a continuous family of steady roll solutions to the Nikolaevskiy equation within a specified parameter regime. Crucially, it demonstrates that these steady rolls are spectrally unstable using advanced computer-assisted mathematical techniques involving Bloch theory and interval arithmetic. The work provides strong mathematical guarantees regarding pattern instability in this physical model.
main_problem: The paper investigates the existence and spectral stability of steady roll solutions within the Nikolaevskiy equation, a model for pattern formation.
main_result: They provide computer-assisted proofs showing that nontrivial, real-analytic steady rolls exist over a continuous two-parameter family and that these rolls are spectrally unstable in a large parameter region.
method: The analysis heavily relies on rigorous computer-assisted proofs using interval arithmetic, parameterized Newton-Kantorovich theorems, and Bloch theory for spectral analysis.
model_or_system: The system is governed by the Nikolaevskiy equation, which models short-wave pattern formation coupled to a neutral long-wave mode. It is analyzed by seeking steady roll solutions $u(x, t) = u(x)$ via a Galerkin approximation.
key_observables: The primary observables are the steady roll solution $u_{q,r}(x)$ and the associated Bloch eigenvalue $\Lambda$, whose real part determines spectral stability.
important_parameters: Key parameters are the wavenumber $q \in [0.9, 1.1]$ and the control parameter $r$ within the range $(1-q^2)^2 < r \leq 4$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the applicability of rigorous bounding techniques (interval arithmetic) and relies on specific truncations (e.g., $M=24$ or $M=48$) for the Bloch spectrum analysis.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the certified covering of the existence region in the $(q, r)$ plane, show the certified lower bound of the real part of the eigenvalue, and present numerical scans of the spectrum.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by establishing the existence of the solution family (Theorem A), rigorously proving its spectral instability over a large domain (Theorem B), and finally analyzing the stability of the long-wave branch (Theorem C).
why_interesting: While the model is classical fluid dynamics, the rigorous mathematical techniques—especially the combination of interval arithmetic with spectral analysis (Bloch theory)—are highly relevant to the rigorous analysis of stability in complex, non-linear physical systems.
